title: These Old Household Brands are Worth a Fortune Now
summary: Some everyday household items have become surprisingly collectible. Before you clear out a cupboard or attic box, see which old finds may be worth a second look.

items.title: Le Creuset
paragraphs: As well as their gorgeous, gradient designs which come in a broad range of colors, Le Creuset products are known for their effectiveness in retaining temperature and lasting an age.
The company has been perfecting its range for over 100 years, but you won't be able to snag many of its products on the cheap.

items.title: KitchenAid
paragraphs: KitchenAid has come a long way since it was founded in 1919, as the company's stand mixers are now a common fixture in homes across the world.
They have gone from making mechanical egg-beaters to creating a must-have appliance for any fashionable kitchen. You should expect to pay a fair bit if you want one, though.

items.title: Tefal
paragraphs: Tefal is known as the pioneer of the non-stick pan, with a red dot that shows you when the pan is hot enough to start cooking.
Tefal pans from the brand's early days in the 1970s are popular with cookware collectors as they were important in the rise of non-stick cooking.

items.title: Salter
paragraphs: Salter began in the late 1760s when their founder, a spring-maker named Richard Salter, started manufacturing the first spring-based scales.
The company thrived ever since, experiencing a further rejuvenation in the mid-1900s, with many of the products sold throughout this era being popular with collectors.

items.title: Pyrex
paragraphs: Pyrex has been the number-one brand for kitchen glassware for several decades, having first been introduced to the American market in 1915.
The company produces a range of products made from borosilicate glass, which makes them extremely heat-resistant, but also expensive to manufacture.

items.title: Griswold
paragraphs: Griswold cookware products have become sought-after collector's items in recent years, as there are less and less of them available for purchase.
This is because the company went out of business all the way back in 1957, when they were producing high numbers of cast-iron products for the general market.

items.title: Wagner
paragraphs: Wagner started life as a family-run business in 1891, mainly producing cast iron cookware products, which dominated the cookware industry for their first 50 years in business.
The company eventually dissolved in 2008 after various changes of ownership, which is why its products are so highly sought after, and incredibly expensive, today.

items.title: Matfer Bourgeat
paragraphs: Matfer Bourgeat has been in operation since 1814, which guarantees that they know their stuff when it comes to creating high-end cookware.

Boasting a hoard of award-winning collections, Matfer Bourgeat doesn't produce products on the cheap. However, the company offers good value for money in the long-term, as the products don't seem to age.

items.title: All-Clad
paragraphs: All-Clad was created in 1971 in Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, an area which is known as the birthplace of the American steel and aluminium industry.

The company works with some of the best chefs across the USA to tailor their products to the professional market. Thankfully, home cooks can also purchase their products, which while expensive, are top of the range.

items.title: Mauviel
paragraphs: Mauviel originates from the home of great cooking, having been established in France, in 1830. As many of you will know, the French take the cookware they use as seriously as the dishes they create.
Things are not done in half-measures with Mauviel, as the company creates some of the best aluminium cookware on the market. The collections look beautifully rustic, justifying the hefty price tag.

items.title: Hestan
paragraphs: Hestan aims most of its products at professional chefs, offering no-frills, effective cookware made from the highest quality materials.
As you can imagine, this ramps up the price of the company's products, but for good reason, as Hestan works with the best American chefs to continuously evolve its designs.

items.title: Emerson
paragraphs: One of the more surprising items to consistently do well at auction are electric fans, which can fetch up to $350 if in good condition.
Emerson is one of the most popular brands for household fans, with 1950s models being highly sought after by collectors.

items.title: Demeyere
paragraphs: Established in Belgium, in 1908, Demeyere has become one of the highest-regarded cookware manufacturers in the world, constantly producing new and innovative designs.
The heat retention and easy-clean nature of Demeyere's products makes them a hit with both professional chefs and eager home cooks.

items.title: Amoretti Brothers
paragraphs: Amoretti Brothers started business in the beautiful city of Turin, Italy, with the aim of producing high-end, handmade products that would last a lifetime.
They produce kitchenware, bathroom features, and accessories, all made to the highest standard, with the prices of their various ranges reflecting their quality.

items.title: Ruffoni
paragraphs: Ruffoni has developed an excellent reputation for its handcrafted, luxury cookware, which has been manufactured in Italy since 1931.
The attention to detail on Ruffoni's pans is second to none, with the brand utilizing the triple-layer construction method, guaranteeing the durability and effectiveness of the product.

items.title: Malm
paragraphs: Futuristic vibes were the vibe of choice back in the 1950s, with people cramming space-age-looking objects into their homes. The fad died out, and these objects soon became few and far between.
What goes around comes back around though, and a large market is beginning to develop for the '50s look once again. The most sought-after item? The Malm fireplace, that sells for up to $5000.

items.title: Staub
paragraphs: Staub is commonly seen as Le Creuset's main slow-cooker competitor, and when you look at the two products side by side, it's easy to see why.
Older Staub slow-cookers are sought after by collectors, with their attractive colorways, durability, and ability to retain heat playing an important part in their popularity.

items.title: Mathmos
paragraphs: Back in the '60s, the lava lamp was the epitome of cool, being a new, fancy invention that looked like it had landed on earth from the future.
Vintage Mathmos lava lamps are flying back into fashion, with collectors lining up to adorn their ''60s-inspired living rooms with a dash of futuristic intrigue.

items.title: Hazel-Atlas
paragraphs: After the conclusion of the Second World War, parties in America became more common, with glassware production going through a golden age as a result.
One of the most notable glassware companies of this era was Hazel-Atlas, which has since gone out of business, greatly inflating the price of the company's glasses and barware.

items.title: Telechron
paragraphs: Art-deco-style wall clocks were all the rage back in the 1930s and '40s. Alas, we live in an age of minimalism, where such decorations aren't overly desired.
That is unless you are a collector, as they tend to be more than willing to part with over $1,000 to get their hands on an old Telechron clock.

items.title: Hubley
paragraphs: Hubley was established in 1894 as a wooden toy company, but they eventually moved into cast iron, making doorstops and other home accessories.
These became a mainstay in the American home, before eventually going out of fashion. Hubley doorstops are now a collector's item and can sell for up to $10,000!

items.title: Ball
paragraphs: Ball is a great example of a historic American company that was able to establish an early dominance over its chosen field, glassware.
The company's most popular item in the early 1900s was the Mason upside-down jar, which could grind coffee and act as a storage container. These jars now cost around $1,000 secondhand.

items.title: Royal
paragraphs: There were a handful of typewriter brands available before they started to become obsolete. Perhaps the best of them all was Royal.

Royal used to pride itself on the fact that their typewriter was the quietest on the market, and that may well have been the case. Public appreciation for Royal typewriters persists to this day, and that's reflected in their resale price.

items.title: Handel
paragraphs: Handel lamps are very reminiscent of what you'd see in an early 1900s period drama, with their drooping, stained-glass shades.
The company was one of many unfortunate victims of The Great Depression, closing its doors in 1936. There are still many of these lamps floating from owner to owner, with ever-increasing pricetags.

items.title: RCA
paragraphs: Once upon a time, radio was king, providing the main source of entertainment in households all across the globe.
One brand that seemed to rule them all in the US was RCA. If you want an RCA Victor radio for your house today, be prepared to shell out at least $2,500.

items.title: New England Glass Company
paragraphs: Perfume bottles from the New England Glass Company unsurprisingly fetch a few hundred dollars in today's market, not just because of their beauty, but because the company rebranded in 1892.
It changed its name to Libbey and started to produce a higher quantity of products, meaning its glassware, mostly perfume bottles, is worth more under its former name.
items.imageAlt: New England Glass Company household brand collectible

items.title: Tiffany & Co.
paragraphs: While it is usually regarded as a jeweller nowadays, Tiffany & Co. has been producing homeware since 1837, some examples of which are now worth a fortune.
To purchase full set of Tiffany & Co. silver cutlery, you will need to have a few thousand dollars to spare.

items.title: Thonet
paragraphs: Thonet furniture is still going strong today, thanks to its high-level craftsmanship and quality. The company has been around for a fair while though, starting up in 1819.
Early Thonet chairs are worth a fortune, both because of their age and also because the bent-wood style they used is legendary among furniture enthusiasts.

items.title: Tower
paragraphs: Tower has been in business for over 100 years, crafting excellently made kitchenware and appliances, which are as durable as they are effective.
This longevity has afforded them license to expand, creating higher-quality products for an understandably raised price, despite their previous reputation of being affordable.

items.title: Shreve, Crump & Low
paragraphs: Founded in 1796, Shreve, Crump & Low is North America's oldest surviving purveyor of luxury goods, mostly dealing in jewelry, but historically crafting more practical items, such as cups and jugs.
Any item from the 1800s adorned with the company's name will likely fetch a few hundred dollars at least.
items.imageAlt: Shreve, Crump & Low household brand collectible

items.title: Sharp
paragraphs: The home electronics industry has progressed so quickly, that items from the '90s look like ancient relics. The aren't many electronics brands more closely associated with the decade than Sharp.
They manufactured a whole host of, what was at the time, high-tech items, including boomboxes and televisions. Try and snag an old Sharp boombox and you'll be paying a lofty fee though.

items.title: CorningWare
paragraphs: When CorningWare introduced their ceramic cookware in the '50s, it was pretty revolutionary, as they could withstand thermal shock of up to 820 Fahrenheit.
While plenty of other companies have caught up and can produce similar products, old CorningWare kitchen items tend to be worth a good few dollars if kept in good condition.

items.title: Oster
paragraphs: Vintage electronics will skyrocket your energy bills and possibly blow up in your face when you try to turn them on, but they still look pretty cool.
Early electronic items from brands such as Oster, a company that was founded in 1928, will sell for a hefty amount, though examples serve more as historical relics than usable appliances.

items.title: Robert Welch
paragraphs: Robert Welch's Campden pans first came onto the market in the 1950s, and they have been a firm choice for enthusiastic home cooks ever since.
They may not be fighting it out at the top with many of the major brands, but the undeniable quality in their products leaves them able to justify their high prices.

items.title: Fiesta Tableware
paragraphs: There aren't many, if any, tableware companies that split opinions like Fiesta, which first came to be in 1936. They were one of the first companies to sell a wide range of brightly colored tableware.
A lot of it was dyed using uranium, which just so happens to be radioactive, so the US government has warned people not to consume food from this potentially dangerous crockery.

items.title: Singer
paragraphs: Back in the 1850s, before the use of plastic in manufacturing went overboard, even sewing machines were a delight to look at, and most notably beautiful were the Singer machines.
As sewing machines evolved, the number of collectors of old Singer machines grew and grew, meaning that nowadays, genuine originals are very difficult to get a hold of.

items.title: IKEA
paragraphs: The Swedish furniture/meatball shop may be well-known for its cheap flat-pack furniture, but a lot of its items have extraordinary resale value.
These items are usually rarer finds from the '60s, '70s, and '80s, but their prices can rise to tens of thousands of dollars.

items.title: Louis Vuitton
paragraphs: Louis Vuitton is expensive at the best of times, but the prices attached to vintage luggage pieces are truly staggering.
It's more than possible that anyone with a vintage Louis Vuitton suitcase sat gathering dust in their attic could be sat on over $20,000.

items.title: Royal Delft
paragraphs: In 1653, Royal Delft was formed in the Netherlands and began producing china in the now famous white and blue coloring.
The value of Royal Delft china increases year on year, with the most valuable products made by the company selling for over $5,000 apiece.

items.title: Stellar
paragraphs: If you're looking for a trusted household name, you can't go too far wrong with Stellar, who has been operating since the 1890s.
A full Stellar 7000 set will set you back a few dollars, but it's a worthwhile investment when you buy a product guaranteed to last.

items.title: LEGO
paragraphs: The famous Danish toy company LEGO is globally known for its plastic bricks that allow children, and adults, to create anything they can dream up.
However, the idea of selling plastic bricks didn't come about until 1949, 13 years after the company was founded. Originally, the company made wooden, pull-along toys which are now worth a fortune.

items.title: Bakelite
paragraphs: Late in the 19th century, phenol formaldehyde resin was discovered by Leo Baekeland, who based his company Bakelite around it.
It was the first form of plastic, so the company was producing a whole range of items to cash in on the new invention. Early Bakelite products, if you can find them, can be very pricey.

items.title: Drexel
paragraphs: For a 30 year period commencing at the end of the Second World War, Drexel was one of the most notable furniture makers in the USA.
Their products were affordable at the time and could blend in with the ever-changeable decor styles between the 40s and the 80s.

items.title: Hoosier
paragraphs: Original Hoosier cabinets revolutionized home cooking when they were invented in 1899, condensing everything the chef of the house could need into one small space.
Hoosier cabinets have since been replicated by just about every furniture company to exist, but there's nothing quite like the - very expensive - original.

items.title: Heywood Wakefield
paragraphs: Unlike a lot of companies that were set up in distinct periods such as the Victorian era, Heywood Wakefield managed to move with the times.
They mastered their furniture products in the art-deco period of the mid-20th century. These pieces are now worth a pretty penny at auction.

items.title: Fire-King
paragraphs: Fire-King is known for making borosilicate products that are resistant to extreme temperatures, hot or cold, similar to Pyrex.
The most valuable Fire-King products sold in auction are the now-vintage, oven-proof jadeite products, in their unmistakable green coloring.

items.title: Broyhill
paragraphs: The Broyhill brand was at its peak during the mid-20th century, meaning you're likely to have come into contact with one of their cabinets at one point or another.
Their products are especially popular with collectors of 1960s pieces and can sell for a lot of money if kept in great condition.

items.title: Miller Knoll
paragraphs: Miller Knoll may not be the most famous of furniture brands, but the pricing of their products made them the number-one choice for offices and waiting rooms across the world.
The company's earlier products can fetch a handsome price, even if they're not always that exciting to look at.

items.title: Carhartt
paragraphs: For most of its existence, Carhartt has been associated with work attire, not fashion. However, things have changed for the brand in recent years.
The mood towards the rugged, heavy-duty workwear has shifted, with the brand setting up shop in cities across the globe, selling clothes for prices that would have once been deemed unthinkable.

items.title: Tala
paragraphs: Tala helped to revolutionize the home cooking experience, creating effective, useful products such as molded baking trays, cooking measures, and icing cones.
The brand's stock has wavered throughout its 120+ year existence, but its vintage items are more in fashion now than ever.

items.title: Tupperware
paragraphs: The Tupperware brand is so famous that a lot of people forget that it's a brand at all, referring to any plastic-made food storage boxes as Tupperware.
The company ceased trading in 2003, but their products are still sold all over the world, with their prices rising year by year.

items.title: Villeroy & Boch
paragraphs: German ceramics manufacturer Villeroy & Boch has been in business since 1748, but their most sought-after range came about in 1967.
The Mexican-inspired 'Acapulco' was a springboard for the company's success in the late '60s. Full sets, if in perfect condition, can be sold for thousands of dollars.

items.title: Morphy Richards
paragraphs: Since 1936, Morphy Richards has been attempting to make kitchen electronics such as blenders, carving knives, and toasters accessible to the masses.
Expect the prices of the company's earliest products, such as the steam iron, to rise as the brand approaches its 100th birthday.

items.title: Alessi
paragraphs: Alessi was in business for around 60 years before they became a household name, mostly due to their employment of recognized designers to create unique-looking products.
The company's art-deco kitchenware items are valuable among collectors, with some being sold for unfathomable prices at auction.

items.title: McCoy Stoneware
paragraphs: As is usually the case, the closing of the McCoy Stoneware doors in 1991 prompted a rise in the price of the company's existing items.
To get your hands on a piece of the brand's famous pottery, you could well end up spending hundreds of dollars.

items.title: Dyson
paragraphs: Just like most electronic items from the '90s, Dyson vacuums have become streamlined and less chunky-looking in recent years.
Such is the popularity of the company, the earliest Dyson vacuums that first entered the market in 1993 are now worth a considerable amount.

items.title: Anchor Hocking
paragraphs: Depression glass was invented in its namesake era during the 1930s, as it was affordable for Americans who were feeling the pinch.
It was mass-produced, and practically being given away for free at one point. However, time has been kind to its value, especially for brands like Anchor Hocking.

items.title: Franciscan Ware
paragraphs: Franciscan Ware's 1950s Starburst range was hugely popular at the time, as households opened up to more color and patterns.
The uniqueness of the range and the vibrance of 1950s household trends have made the Starburst line incredibly popular with collectors.

items.title: Ames Tools
paragraphs: Ames Tools have been used since the early 19th century, and were used to build both the Empire State Building and the Subway system in New York.
Retro Ames Tools products aren't so much meant to be used for their original purpose anymore, but instead are more regarded as historical relics.

items.title: Fenton
paragraphs: The Fenton Art Glass Company was founded in 1905, quickly becoming famous for its semi-translucent 'milk glass' and hobnail pattern design.
These 1960s and 1970s-era pieces are not too easy to find and are highly sought-after by collectors, which has shot their prices skyward.

items.title: Bertazzoni
paragraphs: It's rare for a successful business to retain its family-run status for over 140 years, but that's exactly what Italian kitchenware brand Bertazzoni have done.
It is, of course, the business' age that means their early products are worth a fortune, but the undeniable quality and craftsmanship of the products justifies this money.

items.title: Brabantia
paragraphs: Only a handful of years ago, Dutch residential products company Brabantia celebrated its 100th anniversary, having begun production in the first quarter of the 20th century.
Throughout the company's first century, it prided itself on the durability of its kitchen accessories and utensils, which are still worth a fair amount today.

items.title: Hoover
paragraphs: Before Dyson came along in the 1990s, Hoover was the most famous vacuum cleaner brand, so much so that most people refer to their vacuum cleaner as a Hoover, whatever brand it may be.
Some of the brand's earliest products were not electric, and provide an insight into early home appliances, with their scarcity making them valuable among collectors.

items.title: Lodge
paragraphs: Lodge is another brand that has stood the test of time, along with the cast iron pans and skillets that they manufacture.
The company has been in business since 1896, meaning they have been ever-present throughout the home appliance revolution of the 20th century.

items.title: Harper
paragraphs: Harper, now known as HarperCollins, is a book publisher that has printed some of the most beloved classics to line bookshelves for over a century-and-a-half.
Early editions of books from classic Harper-signed authors can fetch hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars at auction.

items.title: Amana
paragraphs: Amana Radarange microwaves became a roaring success in the late 1960s when they were released, becoming the first compact home microwave on the market.
The importance and pioneering nature of the Radarange is the reason that an original model will cost you a fortune nowadays.

items.title: Corelle
paragraphs: Producing distinctively 70s-looking plates and bowls, Corelle was quickly forgotten about by the 1990s, until nostalgia kicked in after the turn of the millennium.
Not all Corelle kitchenware is worth something, but original 1970s plates are guaranteed to fetch a few dollars if they're kept in good condition.

items.title: Spode
paragraphs: The legacy of Spode Transferware is long and enduring, as the company patented the transferware process, a method that made the decoration of ceramics quick and easy.
As the company was founded in 1776, there are plenty of antique Spode ceramics around, most of them costing a fortune.

items.title: Kerasan
paragraphs: Kerasan has been making bathroom appliances and sanitaryware since 1960, becoming one of the most established names in the industry in the years since.
The Italian brand can be seen in bathrooms across the globe, with their products, although not exciting to most, being long-lasting and high-quality.

items.title: Thomas Crapper
paragraphs: Thomas Crapper's influence on the plumbing scene is often overstated, with his name making him the subject of a wholly inaccurate piece of trivia.

No, he did not invent the toilet. However, he did help advance toilet technology, with his company becoming successful as a result of his innovations. Original Thomas Crapper branded products are now worth a fortune.
